title: How Far Are LLM Research Ideas From Human Ones? A Reverse-Engineering Study
hook: Judging LLM research ideas one at a time (novel? feasible? liked?) hides a bigger question: does the whole distribution of ideas an LLM can produce look like what human researchers actually do?
key_points: For each human paper, the authors reverse-engineer a small set of prior works likely to have inspired its core idea.
LLMs are then prompted to generate a new idea from that same set of prior-work titles and summaries, so human and LLM ideas start from identical inputs.
A two-axis 'research-taste' taxonomy profiles each idea by its opportunity pattern and research paradigm, enabling a distributional comparison rather than single-idea scoring.
LLM-generated ideas cluster disproportionately around 'bridge-like' opportunities and synthesis methods.
Human ideas spread more broadly across ways of framing gaps and constructing contributions.
The gap holds consistently across different LLMs tested, suggesting a systematic narrowing rather than one model's quirk.
content_html: Most evaluations of "can LLMs do research ideation" score one idea at a time: is it novel, is it feasible, would an expert like it. This paper asks a different question — does the whole shape of ideas an LLM tends to generate resemble what human researchers actually produce?
extra_html:
To make the comparison fair, the authors reverse-engineer a small set of prior works likely to have inspired each human paper's core idea, then prompt LLMs to generate a new idea from that identical set of prior-work titles and summaries — so human and machine start from the same inputs. They then classify each idea along a two-axis "research-taste" taxonomy capturing its opportunity pattern (how it frames a gap in the literature) and its research paradigm (how it builds a contribution), letting them compare distributions of ideas rather than judge single instances.

Across ideas generated by several different LLMs, the authors find a consistent gap: LLM ideas disproportionately cluster around "bridge-like" opportunities and synthesis methods — connecting two known things — while the human paper reference set spreads more broadly across other ways of framing problems and constructing contributions. The authors, Ziyu Chen, Yilun Zhao, and Arman Cohan, read this as evidence that strong LLMs can produce a range of reasonable research ideas, but one that's narrower than, and systematically shifted from, human research taste.

related.title: ResearchStudio-Reel: One Extraction, Three Editable Outputs From a Paper
related.hook: Turning a paper into a poster, talk video, and blog is usually done by hand, three times over. ResearchStudio-Reel extracts it once and generates all three — beating even authors' own posters.

flashcards.prompt: Why do the authors reverse-engineer each paper's likely prior-work influences before comparing human and LLM ideas?
flashcards.back_html: So both the human researcher's actual idea and the LLM's generated idea start from the exact same set of prior-work titles and summaries — making the comparison about idea generation itself, not about who had access to better inputs.

flashcards.prompt: What did the two-axis 'research-taste' taxonomy reveal about LLM-generated ideas versus human ideas?

choices.text: LLM ideas cluster disproportionately around bridge-like opportunities and synthesis methods, while human ideas span a broader range of framings
LLM ideas and human ideas were statistically indistinguishable across the taxonomy
LLM ideas were rated as uniformly less novel than human ideas by expert judges

flashcards.explanation_html: The taxonomy profiles each idea by opportunity pattern and research paradigm; across LLMs tested, generated ideas concentrated narrowly on bridging/synthesis approaches, unlike the broader spread of human research taste.

flashcards.prompt: What does this paper's method measure that single-idea novelty/feasibility scoring misses?
flashcards.back_html: It measures the shape of the whole distribution of ideas a system tends to produce, not whether one idea is good — revealing a systematic narrowing in LLM ideation that per-idea scoring wouldn't surface.
